title: Whose is it?
goal: Say who owns what with three forms that follow the thing owned — not the owner — and use an *-s* ending that works just like English, only without the apostrophe.
bekal: the *-s* ending for people's names: *Elins jacka*
nouns for clothes and personal belongings

dialogs.title: Dialogue — I tvättstugan
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning in the shared laundry room. A basket of clothes has been left on top of a machine, and Dian has no idea whose it is.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Elin, är det här din tröja?
lines.literal: Elin, is it here your sweater?

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Nej, min tröja är blå. Den där är nog Oskars.
lines.id: No, my sweater's blue. That one's probably Oskar's.
lines.literal: no, my sweater is blue. that-one there is probably Oskar's.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: De är mina. Tack för att du frågar!
lines.literal: they are mine-plural. thanks for that you ask!

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Var är mitt paraply? Jag hittar det inte.

lines.literal: where is my umbrella? I find it not.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Är det svart? Då står det vid dörren. Ahmad tog det igår.

lines.text: Typiskt Ahmad. Han lånar alltid mina saker.

notes: **The form follows the thing, not the owner.** *Min tröja* (my sweater, an *en*-word), *mitt paraply* (my umbrella, an *ett*-word), *mina saker* (my things, plural). What changes is the ending, and what decides it is the gender and number of **the thing owned**. English "my" never changes, so this is the one genuinely new habit in this unit.

**Hans, hennes, deras, dess never change.** Only *min*, *din*, *vår*, *er* have three forms. The third-person words (*hans*, *hennes*, *deras*) already end in *-s* and stop there: *hans tröja*, *hans paraply*, *hans saker*. That halves the memorizing.
**Vems** means "whose" — and it even looks like it: *vem* (who) + *-s*, exactly like English *who* → *whose*. *Vems är byxorna?* (whose are the pants?), *Vems bok är det här?* (whose book is this?).

**Oskars, Ahmads** — just add **-s** to a name, with no apostrophe. Swedish writes *Oskars tröja*, not *Oskar's tröja* — an apostrophe here is one of the most common mistakes English speakers make. If the name already ends in *-s*, *-x* or *-z*, add nothing: *Lars bok*, *Max jacka*.

**Byxorna är mina** — notice that "pants" in Swedish is always **plural**, exactly as in English (*trousers*, *pants*). So are *glasögon* (glasses) and *pengar* (money — unlike English, where money is singular). Because they are plural, the possessive is plural too: *mina byxor*.

**Nog** means "probably, I guess" — a flavoring word that softens the whole sentence without really being translated. It is a cousin of *väl* and *ju*, and these three little words are what make a sentence sound like a real Swede rather than a textbook.

after: The easiest way to remember it: **a *-tt* ending for *ett*-words, an *-a* ending for plurals**. That is the same pattern as adjectives (*stor / stort / stora*), and you will meet it again in Unit 12.

The noun after a possessive is always in the **indefinite** form: *min bok*, not *min boken*. Ownership already makes it specific, so the definite ending is dropped — just as English says "my book", never "my the book". (Norwegian and Danish allow both orders; Swedish does not.)

after: The third row is easy to miss: when one thing "belongs" to another thing, Swedish prefers *till* or *på* over the *-s* ending — much as English says "the roof of the house" rather than "the house's roof". *Nyckeln till rummet* (the key to the room), *taket på huset* (the roof of the house), *slutet på filmen* (the end of the movie). Using *-s* there — *rummets nyckel* — is grammatical but sounds like formal writing.

The fourth row uses exactly the same forms as the first, just with no noun after them: *Boken är min*, *Huset är vårt*, *Sakerna är mina*. English switches to a different form here (*my* → *mine*, *our* → *ours*); Swedish does not — one less thing to learn.

blocks.text: **En mössa, vantar, en halsduk** are three words you will use every day from October to April. There is a Swedish saying that sums up their whole attitude to weather: *Det finns inget dåligt väder, bara dåliga kläder* — "there's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothes".

Colors are adjectives, so they follow the same pattern: a *-t* ending for *ett*-words, an *-a* ending for plurals. *En röd jacka*, *ett rött hus*, *röda skor*. The word *svart* already ends in *-t*, so its *ett*-form doesn't change.

English
Note
rows: Kan du låna mig hundra kronor?
Could you lend me a hundred kronor?
the person after *låna* tells you which direction
Jag har tappat bort min nyckel.

blocks.text: **Låna** does two jobs that English keeps apart: "borrow" and "lend". What tells them apart is whether there is a person receiving it. *Jag lånar en bok* = I borrow a book. *Jag lånar dig en bok* = I lend you a book. English speakers tend to stumble here at first — not because it is hard, but because one Swedish word has to do the work of two English ones.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 7
items: Give the present tense of the ten verbs from Unit 7 without looking: vakna, duscha, cykla, plugga, handla, laga, träffa, börja, sluta, läsa.
Then combine them with this unit's possessives: *Jag lånar min…*, *Hon tar sina…*, *Vi städar vårt…*
Finally, ask about five things around you: *Vems är…?* and answer yourself with *Den är min* or *Det är mitt*.
